lessons.title: Cleaning and Conditioning of Grains
lessons.body: Before you mill any grain into breakfast cereal, you must clean it. Dirty grain ruins flavor, wears out your mill, and can make people sick. Start with a simple winnowing basket or a mechanical aspirator to blow away chaff, dust, and light seeds. For maize, sorghum, or millet, use a vibrating screen with 2 mm holes to remove sand and stones. A destoner works on density: a slanted vibrating deck with air blowing from below makes heavier stones travel uphill while grain moves downhill. For small-scale operations, a 500 kg/hour destoner costs about $1,200. After cleaning, condition the grain. Conditioning means adjusting moisture so the bran and germ separate easily during milling. For maize, add clean water to raise moisture from 12% to 16%. Mix for 10 minutes in a horizontal mixer, then rest the grain in a bin for 4 to 12 hours. This tempering softens the bran while keeping the endosperm hard. For sorghum, temper to 15% moisture for 6 hours. Millet needs less: 14% moisture for 2 hours. Never skip conditioning if you want clean grits and low fiber in your final cereal. In Africa, where humidity varies, test moisture with a cheap digital meter (around $150) or the traditional salt-and-bottle method: mix 10 g of ground grain with 20 g of dry salt in a sealed jar, shake for 3 minutes, and if salt sticks to the sides, moisture is above 15%. After conditioning, degerminate maize using a degerminator (like a Beall degerminator) or a roller mill set with a 3 mm gap. This removes the germ, which contains oil that turns rancid. For sorghum and millet, the germ is smaller and can stay. Finally, store conditioned grain in clean jute bags in a dry room for no more than 24 hours before milling. Clean and conditioned grain gives you consistent, safe breakfast cereal.

lessons.title: Milling and Grinding Techniques
lessons.body: Milling breaks cleaned, conditioned grain into flour, grits, or meal. Your choice of mill depends on the final cereal texture. For flaked cereals, you need cracked grits, not fine flour. A roller mill with two steel rolls spinning at different speeds (e.g., 500 rpm and 800 rpm) shears the grain. Set the gap to 1.5 mm for coarse grits. For porridge or instant cereals, you need fine flour under 500 microns. A hammer mill with a 1 mm screen does this well. In Africa, many small processors use a plate mill (disc mill) made in Kenya or India. A 10 HP plate mill grinds 200 kg of maize per hour. Set the plates 0.5 mm apart for fine flour, 1.5 mm for meal. Always check the gap with a feeler gauge. Grinding generates heat. If flour temperature exceeds 50Â°C, starch damages and flavor changes. Feed grain slowly and take breaks every 30 minutes. For sorghum and millet, use a stone mill or a pin mill to avoid a burnt taste. After milling, sift the flour. A vibrating sifter with 250-micron and 500-micron screens separates fine flour, middlings, and coarse bran. You can sell the bran as animal feed. For flaking, you need grits between 1 and 2 mm. Pass them through a roller mill again with a 0.8 mm gap, then steam them for 20 minutes at 100Â°C to gelatinize starch. Roll the hot grits between smooth rolls at 10 rpm to flatten into flakes. Dry the flakes at 150Â°C for 10 minutes. In Nigeria, a common setup is a hammer mill for flour and a roller mill for flakes. In South Africa, small plants use a degerminator followed by a roller mill. Always keep spare screens and rolls. Dull rolls crush instead of cut, making uneven particles. Sharpen or replace rolls every 500 hours of use. Proper milling gives you the right particle size for your product, whether you sell fine maize meal or crunchy flakes.

lessons.title: Mixing and Blending of Ingredients
lessons.body: Mixing blends milled grain with other ingredients to make a consistent cereal. For a basic maize porridge, you might mix 80% maize meal, 15% soy flour, and 5% sugar and salt. For a fortified cereal, add vitamins and minerals. Always weigh ingredients on a scale accurate to 1 gram. Never guess. Use a horizontal ribbon blender or a planetary mixer. A 100 kg capacity ribbon blender costs about $3,000 and mixes in 10 minutes. For small batches, a drum mixer works: a 200-liter drum turned at 30 rpm for 15 minutes. Add dry ingredients first, then liquids like oil or water. If you add oil to reduce dust, use 2% vegetable oil and mix for 5 minutes. For extrusion cooking, you need a uniform blend with 12-18% moisture. Add water slowly while mixing. A moisture meter helps. Without one, squeeze a handful: it should hold shape but not drip. For coating, you mix a slurry of sugar, salt, and flavor in water. Use a high-shear mixer to dissolve solids. A common mistake is adding ingredients in the wrong order. Always add minor ingredients (vitamins, colors, flavors) last and mix for at least 5 minutes after. For African cereals like ogi or koko, you ferment maize for 2-3 days before mixing. Fermentation lowers pH to 4.0 and improves flavor. After fermentation, wet-mill the grain, then blend with other flours. If you make instant cereal, blend pre-gelatinized flour with sugar and milk powder. Keep mixing times consistent. Overmixing can heat the blend and damage vitamins. Undermixing gives uneven nutrient levels. Test uniformity by taking 5 samples from different parts of the blender and checking color or salt content. A simple salt test: dissolve 1 g of sample in 10 ml water, add 2 drops of silver nitrate, and compare turbidity. If samples differ, mix longer. Clean your mixer after every batch to avoid allergens and spoilage.

lessons.title: Extrusion Cooking: Principles and Equipment
lessons.body: Extrusion cooking pushes a moist flour blend through a barrel under high heat and pressure, then forces it out a small die. The sudden pressure drop puffs the cereal into shapes like curls, balls, or stars. This is how many breakfast cereals are made. You need an extruder. A single-screw extruder with a 50 kg/hour capacity costs about $8,000. A twin-screw extruder handles sticky blends better and costs $20,000. For African startups, a small single-screw extruder from China or India is common. The key parameters are moisture, temperature, screw speed, and die size. Start with a blend of 70% maize flour, 20% soy flour, and 10% sugar. Add water to reach 15% moisture. Set barrel temperatures: zone 1 at 60Â°C, zone 2 at 120Â°C, zone 3 at 160Â°C. Screw speed at 300 rpm. The die has 3 mm holes. As the blend moves, friction and steam heat it to 150Â°C. Starch gelatinizes and protein denatures. When it exits the die, water flashes off and the product expands. Collect the extrudates on a conveyor and dry them at 120Â°C for 15 minutes to reduce moisture to 3-5%. Without proper drying, extrudates become soggy. For colored cereals, add natural colors like beetroot powder or turmeric at 0.5% in the blend. For flavored cereals, coat after extrusion. Always preheat the extruder for 10 minutes. Start with a low feed rate, then increase. If the extruder jams, stop and clean the die. Never put your hands near the die when running. In Kenya and Nigeria, extruded snacks and cereals are popular. You can make puffed maize balls, soy-fortified curls, or millet-based rings. Test expansion by measuring the diameter of 10 extrudates. Good expansion is 2-3 times the die diameter. If expansion is low, increase moisture or temperature. If product is too dark, lower temperature. Keep records of settings for each product. Extrusion is fast, continuous, and gives you many shapes from the same blend.

lessons.title: Drying and Toasting Methods
lessons.body: After extrusion, flaking, or mixing, cereal needs drying or toasting to reach 3-5% moisture for crunch and shelf life. Drying removes water; toasting adds flavor and color. For drying, use a tray dryer, fluid bed dryer, or solar dryer. A solar dryer with a black mesh tray and a glass cover can dry 20 kg of cereal in 6 hours on a sunny day. For larger scale, a fluid bed dryer at 80Â°C for 10 minutes dries 100 kg per batch. A tray dryer with forced air at 70Â°C takes 30 minutes. Always spread cereal in a thin layer, no more than 3 cm deep. Stir every 10 minutes for even drying. Test moisture by weighing 10 g of sample, drying in an oven at 105Â°C for 3 hours, and weighing again. The weight loss is moisture. For toasting, use a rotary toaster or a belt toaster. A rotary toaster at 200Â°C for 2 minutes gives a golden color and nutty flavor. For flaked cereals, toast at 180Â°C for 3 minutes. For puffed cereals, toast at 220Â°C for 1 minute. In Africa, you can use a modified drum roaster for coffee. Set it to 180Â°C and turn at 30 rpm. Watch for smoke; if it smokes, lower heat. Toasting too long makes bitter cereal. Toasting also kills microbes. After toasting, cool the cereal to room temperature on a clean tray. Never pack hot cereal; condensation makes it soggy. For sugar-coated cereals, dry the coating before toasting. For honey-coated cereals, toast at lower temperature (150Â°C) to avoid burning honey. Store dried cereal in airtight containers or foil bags with a desiccant. A 500 g bag of cereal should have less than 5% moisture. If you live in a humid area, use a dehumidifier in the packing room. Always check moisture before packing. A cheap moisture meter costs $150. Without it, bite a piece: it should snap, not bend. Proper drying and toasting give you a safe, crunchy product that lasts 6 months.

lessons.title: Coating and Enrobing Technologies
lessons.body: Coating adds sugar, flavor, color, and nutrients to the outside of cereal. Enrobing covers the cereal completely with a thin layer. For sugar coating, make a syrup with 60% sugar, 30% water, and 10% honey or glucose. Heat to 110Â°C. Use a rotating coating drum (like a cement mixer but food-grade). Put 10 kg of dried cereal in the drum. Spray the syrup at 5 ml per second while the drum turns at 20 rpm. After spraying, add 1% flavor powder (e.g., vanilla, cinnamon) and tumble for 2 minutes. Then dry the coated cereal at 80Â°C for 10 minutes to set the coating. For chocolate coating, melt 1 kg of cocoa butter with 1 kg of cocoa powder and 2 kg of sugar. Temper the chocolate to 32Â°C. Pour over 5 kg of cereal in a drum and tumble until coated. Cool at 15Â°C for 10 minutes. For yogurt coating, mix 1 kg of yogurt powder with 500 g of sugar and 200 ml of water. Spray and dry. For savory coatings, use 2% salt, 1% onion powder, and 1% garlic powder in a starch slurry. Spray and toast at 150Â°C for 5 minutes. For enrobing with a continuous curtain, use an enrober machine. A small enrober costs $5,000. It pumps coating over a wire mesh belt carrying cereal. Excess coating falls through and is recycled. For small-scale, hand-dipping works: hold a handful of cereal in a sieve, dip into coating, and shake off excess. Always coat after drying and toasting. Never coat wet cereal. Coatings add 10-30% weight. Keep coating room at 20Â°C and 50% humidity. Too humid, coating sticks. Too dry, coating cracks. In Africa, popular coatings are honey, sugar, chocolate, and moringa. Moringa coating adds nutrition. Use 5% moringa leaf powder in the syrup. Test coating adhesion by dropping 10 pieces from 30 cm onto a hard surface. If coating flakes off, add more syrup or dry longer. Store coated cereal in foil bags to prevent moisture. Coating makes cereal attractive and tasty, but it also adds cost. Calculate your coating cost per kg before selling.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Cereal Processing Fundamentals for African Breakfast Cereal Enterprises

This practical reference consolidates the six core lessons of the Cereal Processing Fundamentals module into a single, business-focused guide for African cereal processors. Whether you are running a small mill in Kumasi, a maize flake line in Nairobi, or a fortified porridge blending operation in Lilongwe, the fundamentals below determine your yield, your product consistency, your energy costs, and ultimately your margin. The emphasis here is on decisions that affect money: raw material losses, throughput, downtime, and compliance with food safety requirements that buyers and regulators increasingly demand.

Stage 1 & 2: Cleaning and Conditioning â Protecting Yield and Equipment

In African processing, grain arrives with stones, sand, chaff, metal fragments, and sometimes aflatoxin-contaminated kernels. Cleaning is not optional â it protects your mill, your customer, and your brand. A typical cleaning train for maize, sorghum, or millet includes aspiration (removes light chaff), sieving (removes oversized and undersized material), destoning (removes stones by density), and magnetic separation (removes ferrous metal). For small and medium enterprises (SMEs), a combined destoner-aspirator unit is often the most cost-effective first investment because stone damage to mill plates is a leading cause of unplanned downtime.

Conditioning (tempering) adjusts grain moisture to optimise milling. For maize dry milling, target moisture is typically 14â16%; for sorghum and millet, 12â14% is common. Tempering time ranges from 15 minutes to several hours depending on grain hardness and desired particle size. In humid African climates, conditioning is often about reducing moisture rather than adding it, especially before storage. Under-conditioned grain produces excessive fines and broken grits; over-conditioned grain gums up mills and reduces throughput.

Table 1: Typical Conditioning Parameters for Common African Cereals
Cereal Target Moisture (%) Tempering Time Typical Product Key Risk if Off-Spec
Maize (white/yellow)14â1630 min â 4 hFlakes, grits, porridge flourFines, low yield, plate wear
Sorghum12â1415 min â 2 hExtruded snacks, porridgeHard grits, high energy use
Millet (pearl/finger)12â1415 min â 1 hFlour blends, maltSticky milling, screen blockage
Rice (broken)13â1520 min â 1 hRice flakes, puffed riceExcess breakage, poor puffing
Wheat15â174 â 24 hExtruded cereals, flourUneven hydration, tough bran

Source: Compiled from FAO (1995) "Sorghum and Millets in Human Nutrition," FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin No. 129, and Kent, N.L. & Evers, A.D. (1994) "Technology of Cereals," 4th ed., Pergamon Press.

Stage 3 & 4: Milling and Grinding â The Yield-Critical Step

Milling is where your raw material becomes saleable product, and where most SMEs lose money. Hammer mills are common across Africa for their low capital cost and versatility, but they produce a wider particle size distribution than roller mills. For breakfast cereals, consistency matters: uneven particle size leads to uneven cooking, uneven drying, and rejected batches. If you are producing extruded flakes or puffed cereals, invest in a roller mill or a pin mill with a classifier, or at minimum add a sifter to recycle oversize material.

Energy consumption is a major cost driver. In many African countries, electricity tariffs for agro-processing range from USD 0.10â0.25 per kWh, and milling can account for 30â50% of total processing energy. Regular maintenance of mill plates or hammers â sharpening or replacing every 200â400 tonnes of throughput â can reduce energy use by 10â20% and improve particle size consistency.

Table 2: Milling Equipment Comparison for African Cereal SMEs
Mill Type Typical Capacity (kg/h) Capital Cost (USD, indicative) Particle Size Consistency Best Use Case
Hammer mill200â2,0001,500â8,000LowâMediumPorridge flour, animal feed
Plate mill (burr)100â800800â4,000MediumSmall-batch flour, millet
Roller mill500â5,00015,000â80,000HighFlakes, extruded cereals
Pin mill300â2,5008,000â30,000HighFine flour, instant porridge
Disc mill (attrition)150â1,0001,200â6,000MediumWet milling, nixtamalised maize

Source: Indicative ranges compiled from FAO/UNIDO agro-processing equipment guides and manufacturer specifications (e.g., Alvan Blanch, Muharata, and local East/West African fabricators). Actual costs vary by country, import duties, and currency.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Dust Explosion and Aflatoxin Risk

Cereal dust (especially from maize, wheat, and rice) is combustible. A dust cloud in a confined space â a mill room, a bucket elevator, or a bin â can explode if ignited by a spark, hot surface, or static discharge. In African processing facilities, inadequate ventilation and open electrical fittings are common causes of dust explosions. Always: install explosion venting on bins and dust collectors; use grounded, dust-tight electrical equipment; enforce no-smoking and hot-work permits; and clean settled dust daily. Separately, maize and groundnuts contaminated with Aspergillus flavus can carry aflatoxins, which are carcinogenic and regulated in export markets. Reject mouldy grain at intake and test finished flour for aflatoxin if supplying formal retail or export buyers.

Stage 5 & 6: Mixing, Blending, and Extrusion Cooking

Mixing and blending determine nutritional consistency and product uniformity. For fortified porridge blends â a major growth category in Africa â vitamin and mineral premixes must be distributed evenly. A ribbon blender or paddle mixer with a 10â15 minute cycle is adequate for most SME volumes. Over-mixing can cause segregation of dense premix particles; under-mixing leaves hot spots that fail fortification compliance tests.

Extrusion cooking is the technology behind many puffed, flaked, and shaped breakfast cereals. A single-screw extruder is the entry point for most African SMEs; twin-screw extruders offer better control for high-fibre or high-protein blends. Key parameters are barrel temperature (120â180Â°C), screw speed, feed moisture (14â22%), and die design. Extrusion gelatinises starch, which improves digestibility and texture. In Africa, extrusion is increasingly used for instant maize-soy blends, fortified porridges, and snack pellets.

Stage 7 & 8: Drying and Toasting â Texture, Colour, and Shelf Life

After extrusion or flaking, products must be dried to 3â5% moisture for shelf stability. Fluidised bed dryers are efficient but capital-intensive; tray and tunnel dryers are common in African SMEs but slower and less uniform. Toasting follows drying and develops colour and flavour through Maillard reactions. Over-toasting creates bitterness and acrylamide; under-toasting leaves a pale, under-flavoured product. Target moisture after drying is typically 3â4% for flaked cereals and 4â6% for extruded puffs.

Stage 9 & 10: Coating, Enrobing, and Packaging

Coating adds sugar, honey, vitamins, or flavour. A rotating drum coater with a spray system is standard. For vitamin coating, apply after drying to avoid heat degradation. Packaging must protect against moisture and insects â the two biggest causes of product rejection in African retail. Multi-layer laminated film with a moisture barrier is recommended; simple polyethylene bags are inadequate for long shelf life in humid markets.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Grain intake: Test moisture and aflatoxin; reject mouldy or stone-heavy lots before unloading.
  • Cleaning: Verify destoner and magnet function daily; a single stone can destroy mill plates.
  • Conditioning: Record moisture and tempering time per batch; do not guess.
  • Milling: Check particle size weekly with a sieve stack; replace hammers/plates on schedule.
  • Blending: Run a 10â15 minute cycle and verify premix uniformity with a spot test.
  • Extrusion: Log barrel temperature, feed moisture, and screw speed for every batch.
  • Drying: Target 3â5% moisture; calibrate your moisture meter monthly.
  • Packaging: Use moisture-barrier film and seal integrity checks; label with batch and date codes.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Sorghum and Millets in Human Nutrition (FAO Food and Nutrition Series No. 27)
  • FAO â Small-Scale Cereal Milling and Processing
  • WHO/FAO â Codex Alimentarius: Cereals, Pulses, Legumes and Vegetable Proteins
  • IFPRI â African Food Systems and Value Chain Development
  • UNIDO â Agro-Processing and Food Industry Development Resources

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. Practical parameters should be validated against your specific equipment, local raw material quality, and national food safety regulations.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of conditioning grain before milling?
options: B) To adjust moisture for better bran separation
quiz.explanation: Conditioning adjusts moisture so bran and germ separate easily during milling.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to remove stones from grain based on density?
quiz.explanation: A destoner uses vibration and air to separate heavier stones from grain.

quiz.q: What moisture level is recommended for tempering maize before milling?
quiz.explanation: Maize is tempered to 16% moisture to soften bran while keeping endosperm hard.

quiz.q: Why should you degerminate maize before milling for breakfast cereal?
options: A) To remove oil that turns rancid
quiz.explanation: The germ contains oil that can become rancid and shorten shelf life.

quiz.q: What is a simple traditional method to test grain moisture?
quiz.explanation: Mixing ground grain with dry salt in a jar and shaking shows if moisture is above 15%.

quiz.q: Which mill is best for producing fine flour under 500 microns?
options: B) Hammer mill with 1 mm screen
quiz.explanation: A hammer mill with a 1 mm screen grinds grain into fine flour.

quiz.q: What happens if flour temperature exceeds 50Â°C during grinding?
options: A) Starch damages and flavor changes
quiz.explanation: High heat during grinding can damage starch and alter flavor.

quiz.q: What is the recommended gap for a roller mill to make coarse grits?
quiz.explanation: A 1.5 mm gap produces coarse grits suitable for flaking.

quiz.q: Why should you sift flour after milling?
options: A) To separate fine flour, middlings, and bran
quiz.explanation: Sifting separates particles by size, allowing you to sell bran and use uniform flour.

quiz.q: How often should you sharpen or replace mill rolls?
quiz.explanation: Dull rolls crush instead of cut, so replace or sharpen every 500 hours of use.

quiz.q: What is the first step in mixing dry ingredients for cereal?
quiz.explanation: Accurate weighing ensures consistent nutrient levels and product quality.

quiz.q: Which type of mixer is commonly used for small batches of cereal?
quiz.explanation: A drum mixer turned at 30 rpm for 15 minutes works for small batches.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when adding minor ingredients like vitamins?
options: B) Adding them last and mixing briefly
quiz.explanation: Minor ingredients should be added last and mixed for at least 5 minutes to ensure uniformity.

quiz.q: How can you test mixing uniformity using salt?
options: B) Add silver nitrate and compare turbidity
quiz.explanation: Dissolving samples in water and adding silver nitrate shows if salt is evenly distributed.

quiz.q: Why is fermentation used in some African cereals like ogi?
options: A) To lower pH and improve flavor
quiz.explanation: Fermentation lowers pH to about 4.0 and develops characteristic flavor.

quiz.q: What is the main function of an extruder in cereal processing?
options: B) To cook and puff cereal under pressure
quiz.explanation: Extrusion cooking uses heat and pressure to gelatinize starch and puff the product.

quiz.q: What moisture level is typical for a blend before extrusion?
quiz.explanation: A moisture of 12-18% is needed for proper extrusion cooking.

quiz.q: What happens when extruded cereal exits the die?
options: B) Water flashes off and product expands
quiz.explanation: The sudden pressure drop causes water to flash off, puffing the cereal.

quiz.q: Why is drying after extrusion important?
options: A) To reduce moisture to 3-5% for crunch
quiz.explanation: Drying removes excess moisture, giving a crunchy texture and longer shelf life.

quiz.q: What is a good expansion ratio for extruded cereal?
quiz.explanation: Good expansion is 2-3 times the die diameter, indicating proper puffing.

quiz.q: What is the target moisture content for dried breakfast cereal?
quiz.explanation: Cereal should be dried to 3-5% moisture for crunch and shelf stability.

quiz.q: How can you test if cereal is dry enough without a meter?
options: A) Bite a piece; it should snap
B) Squeeze it; it should hold shape
quiz.explanation: A dry piece snaps when bitten, while a moist piece bends.

quiz.q: What temperature is recommended for toasting flaked cereals?
quiz.explanation: Flaked cereals are typically toasted at 180Â°C for 3 minutes.

quiz.q: Why should you cool cereal before packing?
options: A) To prevent condensation and sogginess
quiz.explanation: Packing hot cereal causes condensation, making it soggy.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of enrobing?
options: A) To cover cereal completely with a coating
quiz.explanation: Enrobing applies a continuous coating over the cereal surface.

quiz.q: What sugar concentration is typical for a coating syrup?
quiz.explanation: A 60% sugar syrup is common for coating cereals.

quiz.q: How can you test coating adhesion?
options: A) Drop pieces from 30 cm and check for flaking
quiz.explanation: Dropping coated cereal shows if the coating flakes off easily.

quiz.q: What is a popular nutritional coating in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Moringa leaf powder is used as a nutritious coating in some African cereals.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid coating wet cereal?
options: A) Coating will not stick properly
C) Cereal will become too hard
quiz.explanation: Coating adheres best to dry cereal; wet cereal causes uneven coating.

quiz.q: What is the recommended humidity for a coating room?
quiz.explanation: A relative humidity of 50% prevents coating from sticking or cracking.
